title: Ordering without a shared clock: logical clocks and IDs
goal: By the end, you can stamp events so that a cause always sorts before its effect, with Lamport and hybrid logical clocks, say what neither stamp can tell you, choose an id scheme by the order it really promises, and fix an id generator whose clock steps back.
opening:
Picture a simple group chat app that sorts messages by the time on the phone that sent each one. One friend asks "Dinner at eight?" and another answers "Yes, see you there!" On your screen, the answer shows up above the question. The second phone's clock runs a minute slow.

Sorting by time feels like the safe choice, because time seems to be the one thing everyone agrees on. Computers don't, quite. No two clocks agree exactly, and a message between two machines can take less time than the gap between their clocks.

In Leases, locks and fencing tokens, one counter numbered every lock holder, and the bigger number won. Here no single counter sees every event. In this lesson, we'll stamp events by counting them instead of reading clocks. Then we'll add the clock back in a careful way, and find out what the order of an id really promises. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Machine A approves a card payment and sends a message to machine B, which completes the payment 5 ms later. A's clock is 40 ms ahead of B's, and each machine stamps its event with the time of day from its own clock. Sorted by those stamps, which event comes first?
options: The approval: it really happened first
The completion, by 35 ms
They tie, because clocks are kept within a millisecond of each other
It depends on which machine does the sorting
warmup.why: A's stamp is the real time plus 40 ms. B's is the real time, and B's event is only 5 ms later, so B's stamp is 35 ms smaller. Stamps from two machines' clocks come out in the right order only when the gap between the events is bigger than the gap between the clocks. Clocks are often kept within milliseconds, but Clocks you can't trust showed that nothing promises it. Who sorts doesn't matter: the stamps are already wrong.

sections.h: A clock's timestamp can put the effect before its cause
sections.body:
Let's set up the payments program. A card payment happens in two steps. First the shop's card reader asks for approval, and the bank sets the money aside. Later the money really moves, which the labs call the capture. Different machines handle the two steps, and we'll call each one a node, the usual name for one computer in a system of many.

Node A approves payment `pay-81723` at 10:00:00.100 and sends a message to node B, which captures the payment 5 ms later. A's clock runs 40 ms ahead of B's. That's well within what NTP, the service that keeps computer clocks close to the right time over the internet, can leave between two servers (Clocks you can't trust). So A stamps the approval 10:00:00.140, and B stamps the capture 10:00:00.105. Sort the events by timestamp and the capture comes first, 35 ms before the approval it depends on. A program that replays events in timestamp order would capture a payment that hasn't been approved yet.

That happens whenever the skew, how far apart two clocks are, is larger than the time a message takes between them. It's the group chat from the opening. The Try it measures it on made-up histories (lists of events and messages) with 4 nodes and messages that take 1 to 20 ms. When the clocks agree, no message ever arrives before it was sent. With up to 10 ms of skew, 153 of 1,950 messages do, and with 50 ms, a third of them.

What order do we actually need? Causes before their effects, and that order has a name: **happens-before**. Event a happened before event b, written a → b, in three cases:

- a and b ran on the same node, and a came first;
- a is the sending of a message, and b is its arrival;
- a chain of such steps leads from a to b.

In the chat, the question happened before the answer, because the second friend read it first. If neither a → b nor b → a, the two events are concurrent: neither could have known about the other, whatever the clocks say. Happens-before is about what could have influenced what, not about time.

So the rule a timestamp T has to follow fits on one line: if a → b, then T(a) < T(b). Concurrent events may come out in either order, as long as everyone agrees on it. Wall-clock time, the time of day a clock shows, breaks that rule. It also does something we'd like to keep, which is to say roughly when an event happened.

Every scheme in this lesson builds on one idea. A cause can reach an effect only along one node's own events or along a message. Suppose a timestamp only grows along both: each node counts its events, and every message carries the sender's number, so the receiver jumps past it. Then an effect can never get a smaller timestamp than its cause, whatever the clocks do. Next, we'll build the simplest clock that works this way.

aside.title: Why not keep the clocks closer?
aside.body: Better clock syncing makes the problem rarer, and it's worth doing. But no syncing gives a limit you can count on everywhere. A clock that loses contact with its time service drifts a little further every day, and a correction can step a clock without warning (Clocks you can't trust). A stamp that follows the messages can't be broken by a bad clock at all.

try.title: Count effects stamped before their causes
steps: Run the demo from the `labs` folder. For each amount of clock skew, it makes up 20 histories of 300 events on 4 nodes. It finds every pair where a happened before b, using vector clocks (the second section explains them), and counts the pairs where b's wall-clock stamp is earlier than a's.

Before you look: at what skew do backward messages start, given that messages take 1 to 20 ms? What will the Lamport and HLC columns say? (Those are the clocks of the next two sections; guess anyway.)
try.expect:
```text
max skew   messages backwards   causal pairs backwards   Lamport backwards   HLC backwards
    0 ms       0 of  1954          0 of   773170                   0               0
    2 ms      17 of  1950         35 of   772763                   0               0
    5 ms      56 of  1950        134 of   772763                   0               0
   10 ms     153 of  1950        533 of   772763                   0               0
   20 ms     322 of  1950       2369 of   772763                   0               0
   50 ms     657 of  1950      15890 of   772763                   0               0
```

With clocks that agree, nothing goes backwards. From 2 ms of skew, some messages "arrive" before they were sent: the ones faster than the skew between their two nodes. With 50 ms, about a third do. Causal pairs, the pairs where one event happened before the other, include long chains through several nodes. They go wrong less often, but they go wrong. Lamport and HLC stamps never do, whatever the skew. That's the property the lab's tests check on random histories.

sections.h: Lamport timestamps: count events, and jump past every message
sections.body:
Leslie Lamport described the simplest version in 1978. Every node keeps a counter that starts at 0:

- Before each local event (one that involves no message) or send, the node adds 1 and stamps the event with the counter.
- A message carries the sender's stamp.
- On arrival, the node sets its counter to the larger of its own and the message's, then adds 1 for the receive.

A stamp is the pair (counter, node id), where the node id is each node's own number. To compare two stamps, compare the counters, and if they are equal, put the smaller node id first. That tie-break makes the order total: any two events from any nodes have a definite order. The stepper builds one with three nodes: auth approves payments, capture moves the money, and ledger keeps the balances. Capture's counter is 1 when a message stamped 2 arrives, so the receive becomes 3, and everything capture does afterwards sorts after the approval.

It works because along one node's events the counter only grows, and across a message the receiver ends up strictly above the sender. A chain from a to b is made of nothing but those two kinds of step, so T(a) < T(b). No clock is involved, so no skew or clock correction can break it.

There are three things it can't do. First, it can't tell "before" from "concurrent". Write L for the Lamport stamp. L(a) < L(b) holds for every a → b, and also for plenty of concurrent pairs. So a smaller stamp means neither "came first" nor "could have caused". Telling them apart takes vector clocks, which the Replication track used for conflicting writes. Every stamp carries one counter per node, and two stamps are compared entry by entry. If each has a larger entry somewhere, the events are concurrent. The price is size: a counter for every node, in every stamp.

Second, a Lamport stamp has nothing to do with time, so you can't ask for everything after 10:00. A node that rarely hears from others counts at its own pace, and its counter can be thousands away from a busy node's.

Third, concurrent events are ordered by counter and node id, so two events that a person saw happen in one order can be stamped in the other. The Try it prints pairs like that, and the last section shows what they cost.

Lamport's clock gets causes right and forgets time. Next, we'll add the time back without losing the guarantee.

steps: Run the demo. It prints a 10-event history on 3 nodes, with each event's wall clock, Lamport stamp and vector clock. Cover the Lamport column first and work it out yourself from the rules, row by row. Rows are in real-time order, and `recv m1` gets the stamp carried by `send m1`.
Look at row 6: `n1 recv m1` has a wall clock of 18 ms, earlier than the 33 ms at which m1 was sent. What does its Lamport stamp say instead?
Read the pairs at the end. Run it again with `-Pargs='5'` for another history.

```text
 8  n0    recv m2         38  (5,0)    [5,0,2]
 9  n1    local           21  (5,1)    [3,2,0]
concurrent pairs (vectors incomparable): 20. Lamport orders every one; some against real time:
  #3 (2,2) sorts before #2 (3,0), but #2 happened first; [3,0,0] and [1,0,1] are incomparable
  #6 (4,1) sorts before #5 (4,2), but #5 happened first; [1,0,3] and [3,1,0] are incomparable
  #7 (4,0) sorts before #5 (4,2), but #5 happened first; [1,0,3] and [4,0,0] are incomparable
```

Row 6 shows the jump: n1 had counted nothing, the message carried 3, so the receive gets 4. That puts it after the send in Lamport order, even though n1's clock says 18 ms. The last lines show what Lamport can't do. #2 happened before #3 in real time, yet (2,2) sorts before (3,0). Nothing is wrong with that, because neither could have influenced the other: their vectors are incomparable, which only a vector clock can tell you.

sections.h: Hybrid logical clocks: clock time when the clocks agree, a counter when they don't
sections.body:
In 2014, Sandeep Kulkarni, Murat Demirbas and colleagues asked for both: Lamport's guarantee and a value close to the wall clock, in 64 bits, the size of one ordinary whole number in Java. The first attempt that comes to mind keeps one number l per node and bumps it with Lamport's rule, using the clock reading pt (physical time) as a floor: l = max(l + 1, the message's l + 1, pt). Their paper shows that this fails. Every bump adds one unit, and messages going round a loop of nodes can push l ahead of real time without limit.

The fix splits the stamp in two. l is the largest wall-clock reading the node has heard of, its own or one carried in a message. c counts events that share the same l. The rules:

- Local event or send: l becomes the larger of the old l and the node's wall clock. If l didn't change, c goes up by one; if l moved forward, c starts again at 0.
- Receive: l becomes the largest of the old l, the message's l and the wall clock. Then c continues the count of whichever l won. If the old l and the message's l tied, c is one more than the larger of their two c values. If only one of them won, c is one more than that side's c. If the wall clock was ahead of both, c is 0.

Compare stamps by l, then c. Every step makes (l, c) larger, and a receive ends up above the message, so happens-before is kept exactly as with Lamport. And because l is always some node's wall-clock reading, it stays close to real time. l is never behind the node's own clock, and never ahead of it by more than the largest disagreement between two clocks, called ε (epsilon). When a correction steps a clock back, l stays put and c counts until the clock catches up, so stamps never go backwards. Packed into 64 bits, 48 for l and 16 for c, a stamp sorts as a plain number. This is a **hybrid logical clock**, or HLC: logical because it counts, hybrid because it also tells the time.

How large does c get? On rented Amazon servers (EC2), with clocks an average of 9 ms apart, the authors measured c = 0 for 65.6% of events, and almost never above 5. With 3 ms, c was 0 for 91.2% of events and 1 for the rest. Across four Amazon regions, data centres in different parts of the world, it was 0 for about 95%, because messages between regions took far longer than the skew.

HLCs are the clock inside several databases. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB, two databases that spread one set of tables over many machines, stamp their transactions (groups of changes saved all together or not at all) with them. MongoDB, a database that stores documents, offers what it calls causally consistent sessions, which keep a client's reads in step with its own earlier writes. To do it, it passes a cluster time back and forth with every operation. The 2019 paper on how it works describes that clock as a hybrid logical clock. The time half means something only while clocks stay close, so these systems police it. YugabyteDB shuts down a server whose clock is more than 500 ms off, by default. CockroachDB does the same when a node's clock is 80% of its 500 ms maximum away from the others'.

Next, we'll look at the ids we give records, which often carry a time of their own.

try.title: See how big the counter gets
steps: Run the demo. For skews from 1 to 100 ms, it replays 20 histories of 500 events through the lab's hybrid clock. It prints how often c is 0, 1 or more, its largest value, and how far l ran ahead of each node's own wall clock.
Predict the row for 3 ms first, using the paper's 91.2% as a guide. Then compare the last two columns with the skew in each row.
try.expect:
```text
max skew    c = 0    c = 1   c >= 2   max c   l - wall clock: max   mean
    1 ms    90.2%     8.9%     0.9%       3                  0 ms    0.0 ms
    3 ms    90.3%     8.9%     0.9%       3                  0 ms    0.0 ms
    9 ms    89.4%     9.4%     1.2%       3                  4 ms    0.0 ms
   30 ms    80.6%    12.7%     6.7%      10                 25 ms    0.7 ms
  100 ms    53.5%    13.7%    32.7%      19                 88 ms   12.4 ms
```

With a few milliseconds of skew, c is 0 for about 90% of events. At 1 and 3 ms, every c above 0 comes from two events in the same millisecond on one node. l never runs ahead of the local clock by more than the skew: 4 ms at 9, 25 ms at 30, 88 ms at 100. At 1 and 3 ms it never runs ahead at all, because a message takes at least 5 ms here, longer than the skew. That's the same reason the paper saw c = 0 for 95% of events across regions. Only at 100 ms, more than the message delay, does c grow often. The simulator counts whole milliseconds, so the shape matches the paper and the exact numbers don't.

sections.h: IDs: who hands out the next number, and what its order promises
sections.body:
Records need ids, and an id is a close relative of a timestamp. It must be unique, and we'd like its order to mean something. Every id scheme answers two questions: who picks the next number, and what does sorting by it tell you?

One counter. A database sequence, such as PostgreSQL's `nextval`, is one place handing out the next number. If one insert (adding a row) finished before another began, the second gets the larger id. That's the strongest order of any scheme here, and it costs a trip to that one place for every id. Two details weaken it. A sequence never goes back, so a cancelled transaction leaves a gap. And a sequence can have a cache (`CACHE 20`): each database connection then takes a block of 20 numbers at a time. Ids from two connections interleave out of time order, the same as handing blocks of ids to different servers.

Random. A UUID is a standard 128-bit id, and version 4, UUIDv4, fills 122 of those bits at random. Any node can make one without asking anybody, two of them are practically never the same, and their order means nothing. In a B-tree, the sorted structure a database uses for its indexes (Storage engines and query execution), every insert lands in a random block of the index.

Time plus something unique. These put milliseconds in the top bits, so ids sort roughly by the time they were made. New rows land at the right-hand end of a B-tree, next to each other, which makes these ids good primary keys, the column a table's rows are looked up by. The figure shows the layouts.

- UUIDv7 comes from RFC 9562 (May 2024), the standard for UUIDs. It holds 48 bits of Unix milliseconds (counted from the start of 1970), the version number, and 74 bits that are random or partly a counter. The RFC asks each generator, the code that makes the ids, to keep its own output increasing, and promises nothing across generators. PostgreSQL 18's `uuidv7()` adds a fraction of a millisecond after the milliseconds, which keeps values increasing within one connection; its documentation promises no order. Kotlin's `Uuid.generateV7()` keeps them increasing within one running program, using a counter, and promises nothing across programs or machines.
- Snowflake, Twitter's 2010 design, is one 64-bit number: 41 bits of milliseconds since its own starting date, 10 bits of machine number, and a 12-bit counter for ids in the same millisecond. That allows 4,096 ids per millisecond per machine. When the clock ran backwards, Twitter's generator refused to make ids until time passed the last one it had issued.
- ULID has 48 bits of milliseconds and 80 random bits, written as 26 characters that sort as text.

At best, all of these order the ids of one generator. Across machines, their order is the order of the machines' clocks. In the Try it, the capture made on a machine 40 ms behind gets a smaller id than the approval that caused it. On one machine, a clock that steps back makes a naive generator repeat ids. The lab fixes that the way an HLC would: never use a millisecond older than the last one, and when 4,096 ids have used up a millisecond, borrow the next. Ids can't promise causes before effects across machines. Next, we'll meet an order that even stamps can't promise.

The naive generator walks back through milliseconds it has already used, with sequence 0 each time, so its last three ids are exact copies of its first three. Neither can fix the last line: the capture, made on the machine whose clock is 40 ms behind, sorts before the authorization (the approval) that caused it.

sections.h: When no message connects two events: one counter for real-time order
sections.body:
Lamport stamps and HLCs promise one thing: a new stamp is larger than every stamp the node has heard of. When no message connects two events, they promise nothing about their order, even if a person watched one happen after the other.

The company's fraud team puts a hold on payouts to shop M-0042 while they look into it. The hold commits, which means it is saved for good, at 1,000 ms on the merchants shard (the labs call shops merchants), with HLC (1000, 0). A shard is one of several databases that each hold part of the data (the Partitioning track), and this one holds the shops. The company's program then sends the shop a webhook, a message to the shop's own computer saying something changed. The shop's computer reacts by asking for a payout. The request commits on the payouts shard 30 ms later, and that shard's clock is 80 ms behind, so the payout gets HLC (950, 0).

The rule is that a hold blocks every payout created after it. By timestamp, the payout came first, so it is paid. In real time, the hold came first, by 30 ms, and the payout was a reaction to it. The link between them ran through the shop's computer, outside the system, and no stamp went with it. Lamport stamps do no better: the payouts shard has counted fewer events, so its stamp is lower still. It's the group chat again, with the question read on a phone and the answer typed on a laptop.

There are three ways out. The first is to carry the stamp across the gap. Put the hold's HLC in the webhook, require it back with the payout request, and have the payouts shard treat it as a received message first. MongoDB lets a client do this by moving one session forward to another session's cluster time. It works only if every path carries the stamp, including the ones you don't control.

The second is to take every timestamp from one counter, a **timestamp oracle**. TiDB, a database that spreads over many machines, hands them out from one leader, the one machine in charge of the count: 46 bits of physical milliseconds plus an 18-bit logical counter. Whatever starts after something else has committed gets a larger number, because one node orders them all. The oracle saves a mark ahead of what it has handed out (the demo saves one every 1,000 numbers). So after a failover, when a new leader takes over, it skips numbers but never repeats one. The cost is a round trip to that one leader, in one region, for every transaction.

The third is a clock with a known error bound, plus a wait before each commit until the bound has passed. That's what Google's Spanner does (the last section of Clocks you can't trust).

Which one to use comes down to the order you need:

| You need | Use | It can't |
|---|---|---|
| Unique ids, nothing more | UUIDv4 | sort by time |
| Primary keys that sort roughly by time | UUIDv7, Snowflake, ULID | order ids made on different machines |
| Causes before effects | Lamport or HLC stamps on every message | spot concurrency, or order events no message connects |
| To know which writes were concurrent | Vector clocks | stay small with many nodes |
| Real-time order across unrelated events | One sequence or timestamp oracle, or bounded clocks and a wait | grow past one leader, or skip the wait |

try.title: Pay out a held shop, then stop it
steps: Run the demo. The hold commits on the merchants shard, a webhook reaches the shop, and the shop's computer asks the payouts shard for a payout 30 ms later. The payouts shard's clock is 80 ms behind.
Before you look: which of the three stamps (HLC, Lamport, oracle) orders the payout after the hold?
In `ExternalOrderDemo.kt`, change `real - 80` to `real - 20` and run it again. Why does HLC get it right now?
try.expect:
```text
1,000 ms  hold on M-0042 commits on the merchants shard with HLC (1000,0)
1,030 ms  payout P-9 commits on the payouts shard with HLC (950,0)
        rule check: is P-9 after the hold? false  ->  PAID, although the hold came first
        with Lamport stamps: hold (501,0), payout (301,1), payout after hold: false
        with a timestamp oracle: hold 1, payout 2, payout after hold: true  ->  blocked
        the oracle fails over; the next timestamp is 1001: numbers skipped, none reused
```

The HLC and Lamport stamps both put the payout first, because no message connected the two shards. The oracle orders them by when they asked, one after the other. Its failover jumps to 1,001: the saved mark was 1,000, so the new leader can't reuse a number. With the clock only 20 ms behind, less than the 30 ms between the events, the HLC stamps come out (1000,0) and (1010,0), and the payout is blocked. HLC gets real-time order right only when the gap between events is wider than the skew.

compare.note: Both take the largest of what the node has seen and what the message carries, and both end strictly above the message. That is the whole of the guarantee that causes come first. The hybrid clock adds the wall clock as a third candidate for the largest, and keeps the counter separate from the time, so l stays a real wall-clock reading and c absorbs the ties. Lamport's counter has no units; the hybrid stamp's l is milliseconds you can search by.

steps.say: Ids made in the JVM, the program that runs Kotlin and Java code, such as idempotency keys a client creates before it calls you. Kotlin's generator increases within one running program, here with its counter visible in the fourth group (`73d1`, `73d2`, ...). Across programs, it promises nothing.

Payment events between services: one hybrid clock per service, its stamp in a header of every Kafka message, and `receive` on every message read. (Kafka is a program that passes messages between programs; a header is a small labelled value that travels with a message.) Now the audit can sort a payment's events by `hlc`, and every effect follows its cause.
steps.code:
// producing
val stamp = clock.send().pack()
record.headers().add("hlc", ByteBuffer.allocate(8).putLong(stamp).array())

// consuming
val header = consumerRecord.headers().lastHeader("hlc")
val seen = clock.receive(Hlc.unpack(ByteBuffer.wrap(header.value()).long))
audit.insert(paymentId, event, hlc = seen.pack())

steps.say: Holds and payouts need real-time order, which no stamp from two shards gives. Take both from one sequence with no cache. The hold committed before the payout request began, so the payout's `nextval` is larger, and gaps don't matter.

lab.title: Lamport and hybrid clocks against vector clocks, and a Snowflake that survives a clock step
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed. All 19 fail: the clocks throw `NotImplementedError`, Kotlin's error for code not yet written, and the Snowflake tests fail on the stub's wrong ids.

Read `History.kt`, which is given. `Histories.generate` plays a history of local events, sends and receives on N nodes with skewed wall clocks, from a seed, so the same seed always gives the same history. `vectorStamps` gives the exact happens-before relation; `lamportStamps` and `hlcStamps` replay the history through your clocks.
In `Lamport.kt`, write `compareTo`, `local` and `receive`. `LamportTest` passes, and so does the uniqueness property in `CausalityPropertyTest`.

In `Hybrid.kt`, write `pack`, `unpack`, `local` and `receive` from the rules in the third section. `HybridTest` and the rest of `CausalityPropertyTest` pass. They use jqwik, a testing library that runs one check on hundreds of random inputs: it compares your stamps with vector clocks on random histories, checks the bound on l, and checks that stamps keep growing through a clock step.
Experiment: in `HybridClock.receive`, leave `m.l` out of the largest-of. Run `CausalityPropertyTest` and read the history jqwik reports. Put it back.
hints: `pack` is `(l shl 16) or c.toLong()`; `unpack` is `Hlc(packed ushr 16, (packed and 0xFFFF).toInt())`.
In `local`: `val l = maxOf(last.l, physical())`, then `c = if (l == last.l) last.c + 1 else 0`. Store the result in `last`.
In `receive`, a `when` with four branches, in the order of the KDoc. Check the tie of both l values first.
In `next()`: `var ms = maxOf(clock(), lastMs)`; if `ms == lastMs`, count up and, past `MAX_SEQUENCE`, use `lastMs + 1` with sequence 0.

drill.title: A hybrid clock from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write `local()` and `receive(m)` for a hybrid logical clock with fields `l` and `c` and a `physical()` wall clock. Then write one line on what happens to l when the wall clock steps back.

recap: Wall-clock stamps from two machines put an effect before its cause whenever the skew between the clocks is larger than the time a message takes between them.
Happens-before: events on one node in order, a send before its arrival, and chains of those. The rule for a timestamp: if a happened before b, T(a) < T(b).

Lamport stamps (counter, node) count events and jump past every message: a total order that respects causes, with no notion of time and no way to spot concurrency. Vector clocks spot it, at one counter per node.

Hybrid logical clocks keep Lamport's guarantee in 64 bits whose top 48 are a real wall-clock reading, never more than the skew ahead; the counter is almost always 0 or 1. CockroachDB, YugabyteDB and MongoDB's cluster time use them.

The limit: UUIDv7, Snowflake and ULID sort by time for one generator at most, and no stamp orders events that no message connects. Only one counter (a sequence, TiDB's timestamp oracle) or bounded clocks with a wait give real-time order across them.
closing:
We started with a group chat that showed an answer above its question. Stamps that count events and jump past every message keep a cause before its effect, whatever the clocks say. Ids sort by the clock of whoever made them, and an order that no message carries needs one counter.

Look for this in a shared photo album that several friends' phones and cameras added to. It sorts the pictures by each device's own clock, so a camera whose clock was set wrong puts its photos hours away from the moments they show.

Each order in this lesson kept its promise only under certain conditions. Next, we'll write such conditions down, and see why a proof holds only inside them.

quiz.q: From Clocks you can't trust: a clock correction steps node B's wall clock back 300 ms. Which of B's stamps can now come out smaller than ones it made before the step?
options: Its hybrid logical clock stamps
Its Lamport stamps
Its `System.currentTimeMillis()` readings (the time of day), and anything built only on them, such as a naive Snowflake id
All three
quiz.why: A wall-clock reading follows the step back, and so does an id that copies it. A Lamport clock never reads a clock. A hybrid clock takes the larger of its last l and the wall clock, so after a step back l stays where it was and only c grows. That's why Clocks you can't trust measures durations on a monotonic clock, and why the lab's Snowflake fix borrows the same trick.

quiz.q: Event x on node 1 has Lamport stamp (12, 1) and event y on node 3 has (40, 3). What can you conclude?
options: x happened before y
y did not happen before x; x may have happened before y, or they may be concurrent
x and y are concurrent
Nothing: Lamport stamps from different nodes can't be compared
quiz.why: If y had happened before x, y's stamp would be smaller, so that's ruled out. The rest is open: Lamport stamps give a smaller number to every cause, but also to many events that caused nothing. Only vector clocks tell concurrent from before. Stamps from different nodes compare fine; that's what the node id tie-break is for.

quiz.q: A hybrid clock's last stamp is (5000, 3) and its wall clock reads 5000. A message arrives stamped (5020, 7). What stamp does the receive get?
quiz.why: l is the largest of 5000, 5020 and 5000, so 5020, which came from the message alone. c then continues the message's count: 7 + 1. (5020, 0) would sort below the message's own (5020, 7), breaking happens-before. (5021, 0) is the first attempt from the paper, which adds a unit to l and can drift away from real time without limit. (5000, 4) ignores the message.

quiz.q: Three services insert into one table with primary keys from Kotlin's `Uuid.generateV7()`. What does sorting the table by id give you?
options: Creation order within each running program, and across services only as good as their clocks
Exact creation order across all three services
No order at all: the bits after the timestamp are random
The order the database saved them in, because the database assigns the ids
quiz.why: Kotlin keeps its output increasing within one running program, with a counter, and promises nothing across programs or machines. The top 48 bits are each service's own wall clock, so ids from a service whose clock is behind sort too early. The random bits come after the timestamp, so the order is roughly by time. The ids were made in the services before the insert, so they know nothing of the order in which the database saved them.

quiz.q: Holds live on one shard, payouts on another, and the shop's own computer sits between them. Which change makes "a hold blocks payouts created after it" correct?
options: Replace the shards' hybrid clocks with Lamport clocks
Correct the shards' clocks every minute instead of every hour
Take both shards' commit stamps from one timestamp oracle
Compare the UUIDv7 ids of the hold and the payout instead
quiz.why: The payout request started after the hold committed, so one counter gives it the larger number, whatever the clocks say. No message connected the shards, so Lamport and hybrid clocks have nothing to carry; Lamport is worse, since it ignores time entirely. More frequent clock corrections shrink the skew without bounding it. UUIDv7 ids are wall-clock stamps from two machines, the original problem.

flashcards.front: When did event a happen before event b?
flashcards.back: a and b ran on one node and a came first; or a is a send and b its arrival; or a chain of those leads from a to b. Otherwise they are concurrent.

flashcards.front: The three rules of a Lamport clock?
flashcards.back: Add 1 before each local event or send; send the counter with every message; on arrival, set the counter to max(own, message) + 1.

flashcards.front: What can't a Lamport stamp tell you?
flashcards.back: Whether two events were concurrent (a smaller stamp doesn't mean earlier, or cause), and anything about wall-clock time.

flashcards.front: What are l and c in a hybrid logical clock?
flashcards.back: l: the largest wall-clock reading the node has heard of (48 bits). c: a counter for events that share that l (16 bits).

flashcards.front: How far can an HLC's l be from the node's own wall clock?
flashcards.back: Never behind it, and never ahead by more than the largest skew between two clocks. A clock stepping back leaves l where it was.
Each generator, at best: PostgreSQL 18 within one connection, Kotlin's generateV7 within one running program, JDK 26's ofEpochMillis only if your times do. Nothing across machines.

flashcards.front: What fixes a Snowflake generator whose clock steps back?
flashcards.back: Never use a millisecond older than the last one issued (keep counting the sequence on it), and borrow the next millisecond when 4,096 are used. Twitter's original refused to issue ids instead.

terms.plain: How far apart two machines' clocks are at a given moment.
Event a happened before b if a could have influenced b: same node in order, a send before its arrival, or a chain of those.
Two events where neither happened before the other; no chain of messages connects them.
A (counter, node id) pair from a counter that counts events and jumps past every message it receives.
One counter per node in every stamp; comparing entry by entry shows exactly which events were concurrent.
A stamp of the largest wall-clock reading heard so far plus a counter, which keeps causes first and stays close to real time.
A 128-bit id with Unix milliseconds in its top 48 bits, so ids sort roughly by the time they were made (RFC 9562).
One service that hands out every timestamp from a single counter, so later requests always get larger numbers.

explain_back.prompt: The company's audit report sorts a payment's events by their UUIDv7 ids, and sometimes shows a refund before the capture it reverses. Explain why, and what you'd change.
explain_back.answer: A UUIDv7 id starts with the wall clock of whichever machine made it, and each generator only keeps its own ids in order. The capture and the refund come from different services, so their ids are ordered by two different clocks. If the refund service's clock is behind by more than the time between the two events, its id sorts first, even though the refund was a reaction to the capture. I'd keep UUIDv7 for primary keys, where it's only there so that new rows land next to each other in the index, and add a stamp that follows causes. Each service keeps a hybrid logical clock, puts its stamp in the Kafka header of every event it sends, and calls receive on every event it reads. The refund service has seen the capture's event before it refunds, so the refund's stamp is larger, and the report sorts by that stamp. If the report ever needs to order events that no message connects, like a hold and a payout, a stamp can't help; those need one counter or a check inside one transaction.

deeper.body:
**How big the HLC counter can get.** The paper proves that c stays bounded: roughly the clock skew divided by the least time the clocks move forward while a message travels, plus one. That's why 16 bits are plenty when clocks are within milliseconds and messages take milliseconds, and why a clock that is badly off can make c climb, as the 100 ms row of the Try it shows.

**Vector clocks and version vectors.** Storing a counter per node is fine for a handful of copies of the data and hopeless for every client of a large system. Stores in the style of Amazon's Dynamo keep one entry per copy that coordinated a write, not per client (Concurrent writes: last write wins, version vectors and CRDTs). Systems that must detect concurrency among many writers prune old entries and accept the occasional false conflict.

**How UUIDv7 generators stay in order.** RFC 9562 offers three ways for one generator to keep its ids increasing within a millisecond: a counter in the bits after the time, a random increment, or extra bits of sub-millisecond time. PostgreSQL 18 uses the last, and Kotlin's `Uuid.generateV7()`, still marked experimental, uses a counter. JDK 26's `UUID.ofEpochMillis(ms)` does neither: it takes the time from you, so its output increases only if your times do. ULID's monotonic mode adds one to the 80-bit random part for each id in the same millisecond, and fails if that would overflow. Its spec doesn't say whether one program or the whole system is the scope; in practice it is one generator, like UUIDv7.

**Snowflake's own promise.** Twitter's README described the ids as roughly sorted, within tens of milliseconds as a target, and relied on NTP to keep machines close. The order across machines was only ever as good as the clocks, which is the cost of not asking anyone for the next number.

**Real-time order with clocks.** Spanner's TrueTime returns an interval that the true time is guaranteed to lie in, and a transaction waits out that interval before it reports its commit, so anything that starts afterwards gets a later timestamp. Clocks you can't trust introduced it, and Distributed SQL: Spanner, CockroachDB and Aurora DSQL, in the Consistency and consensus track, comes back to it with CockroachDB's alternative. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 10, treats logical clocks and id generators together with linearizability, the promise that a system behaves as if there were one copy of the data on one timeline.
